title: Stormlight
subtitle: The Shore I Choose · Chapter 9 of 10
content:
The storm came from two directions.

One was the ordinary sea, grey and furious beyond Tideglass Cove. The other blew through an unfinished Threadway, carrying rain that tasted of iron and sending sparks down the old lantern chain.

The first flash of lightning struck a post at the edge of the square. I heard the crack before I saw the wood split.

By the time the bell rang, three houses near the shore had flooded.

Maui stood beside the dock with his fishhook lifted into the wind. A little figure inked over his heart was pointing furiously toward the sea. He watched the waves climb the rocks, and I saw him reach for the kind of answer he knew best.

“I can hold them,” he shouted.

“For how long?”

“As long as I have to.”

“That isn't a measurement!”

The wind took the last word. He reached for my arm, then stopped himself and offered his hand instead. I took it because the path was slippery, not because I had agreed with his plan.

Neri reached us carrying a ledger under their coat. The old paper had already soaked through at one corner. Behind them came two neighbors with ropes, a young carpenter named Arin, and a little boy who would not let go of a tin lunch pail.

“The western row is clear,” Neri reported. “The southern cottages aren't. There's somebody still inside the house with the blue shutters.”

Maui looked at me.

“Go,” I said.

He hesitated.

“I have the drainage map. Neri has the people. We don't need you standing here proving you can carry every job at once.”

A bolt of lightning lit his face. He looked as though he wanted to argue, then glanced at the flooded cottages.

“Tell me what you need when I get back.”

I nodded. “I will.”

He ran toward the house.

I helped Neri unroll the map beneath the bakery awning. The paper had begun to curl, and I put two stones on its corners. Most of Tideglass's drains were older than the buildings above them. I remembered repairing the dock and wondering why the water always returned to the same wall.

Now I saw it.

“The southern ditch is blocked,” I said. “If we clear it, the water will go around the workshop instead of into it.”

Arin frowned at the marks on the map. “That ditch has been dry for years.”

“That's why everybody put things on top of it.”

Neri looked toward the packed sheds.

“Supplies?”

“Some,” I said. “But not the support posts. If we move those, the roof might follow.”

The boy lifted his lunch pail.

“My grandmother's inside,” he said. “She can't walk fast.”

Neri crouched until they were eye to eye.

“What's her name?”

“Anya.”

“Then we'll go get Anya. You stay with Arin and tell him if you see her coming.”

The boy nodded hard.

I watched Neri take the fear seriously without allowing it to become the only thing anyone could do. That was leadership, I thought. Not shouting loud enough for a storm to listen. Making sure a frightened child knew which person would help.

Maui returned with Anya wrapped in a blanket. She was furious about being carried and even more furious about leaving her cooking pot behind.

“You brought me out without my supper,” she told him.

“It was a heroic rescue.”

“It was a damp interruption.”

Maui looked at me, scandalized. “I risked my life.”

“You'll survive the criticism,” I said.

Anya pointed at the flooded street. “The oven's on a stone shelf. You can get the pot when the water goes down.”

“Yes, ma'am,” Maui said.

I had never heard a demigod sound so much like a reprimanded apprentice.

The comedy lasted until the second gust hit.

The unfinished Threadway had opened beneath the rocks, where an inlet should have been. Water from somewhere else pressed into the cove. It wasn't simply overflowing the bank; it was entering faster than the drains could carry it away. The bell under Lanternwell Square rang twice, harsh and uneven, before falling silent.

My stomach tightened. The sound was wrong.

I grabbed the diagram of the old ring. The brass piece that held the doorway in position had slipped out of its groove. Water and wind were moving through the gap.

“Maui! I need you!”

He turned immediately.

“Finally, some appreciation.”

“Bring the long beam from the half-built dock. Not the roof beams. The dock.”

He looked toward the water.

“That beam won't be enough.”

“No. That's why you're coming.”

Together we carried it along the upper path. Maui took the heavier end and let me set the direction. When I told him to stop, he stopped. The first time he had helped me build something, his hands had been everywhere and his patience almost nowhere. The difference now was not that he had become smaller. It was that he was making room.

At the breach I could hear water grinding through stone. The ring was visible between two slabs, half-buried in grit. Sparks crawled along the lantern chain above it.

I made the mistake of reaching down before checking the footing.

A piece of rock shifted beneath my boot.

I caught the edge, but the drop below me opened into black water. For a moment I was again on that first beach, with the world tilting and no past to steady me.

“Jasper!” Maui shouted.

“I'm here.”

“Give me your hand.”

I tried to move. The rock shifted again.

Maui planted his hook across the gap and held it still. Not an order. A brace. Something I could decide to use.

I took his hand.

He pulled me to safer stone, and the force of my own fear hit a moment later. My hands shook as I pressed them against the wet rock.

Maui crouched in front of me.

“Are you hurt?”

“No.”

“Do you need a minute?”

I wanted to say no. I wanted to be useful, brave, the person with the map and the answer. The voice from my old life rose up without a face: If you can help, you have to. Don't make it about you.

“I need one,” I said.

He sat beside me in the rain.

Only a minute. Not because I had earned it, and not because he was withholding help until I recovered. He waited with me while Arin checked the beam and Neri directed another group toward the higher path.

When I stood, my hands were steady enough.

“I have a plan,” I said.

“Good.” Maui rose. “Tell me my part.”

We set the beam against the rock face and tied it back to the old dock posts. The rope was thick and stiff with salt. My fingers remembered the knot before I remembered the lesson, and I let them work. Maui held the current away from the opening with his hook, teeth clenched under the strain.

I measured the brass ring's position by the notch near its inner edge. There was just enough clearance to turn it back.

“Three inches left,” I called.

The ring moved.

“Another inch.”

It caught.

“Hold!”

Maui held.

The brace trembled. I drove the catch into place with the small hammer from my belt. The blow went through my wrist like a sharp bell note. Water rushed past my knees.

Then the Threadway shuddered.

The storm on the other side went silent.

The wind from the sea remained. The rain still beat against our backs. We had fixed one part of a larger disaster, and the ordinary weather had the audacity not to stop.

Maui let his hook drop, breathing hard.

“Did we do it?” I asked.

“We did.”

I laughed once. It was a strange, exhausted sound.

He reached toward my face and waited. I leaned into his palm. His thumb brushed wet hair away from my eyes.

“I was scared,” he said.

“Of the water?”

“Of you disappearing into it.”

I rested my forehead against his for a heartbeat. “Then tell me. Don't turn it into a heroic speech.”

“I was scared,” he repeated.

“Me too.”

It was enough.

We returned to the square and helped count people. Nobody had been lost, but there were bruises, soaked bedding, ruined food, and one smashed boat. The bakery's back wall needed shoring. A family would have to sleep in the meeting hall until their floor dried. Anya demanded her cooking pot again.

Maui retrieved it as promised.

Neri opened the ledger to a dry page.

“Repairs,” they said.

“Drains first,” I replied.

“And the footbridge,” Arin added.

“And the kitchen,” Anya insisted.

We made the list with everyone speaking who had a stake in it. Someone began calling Maui the greatest hero in the vale. He turned, shook his head, and pointed not at himself but at the wet volunteers carrying ropes across the square.

“Talk to the people who made the plan.”

I nearly protested out of habit.

Instead I said, “And don't forget who moved the beams.”

He looked relieved.

That evening, exhausted, we sat on the bakery steps while neighbors laid out borrowed blankets. Lanterns returned one by one, their light reflecting in water that still needed to be carried away in buckets.

“I remembered something in the storm,” I said.

Maui waited.

“I used to think the only reason people needed me was that I could fix things.”

His arm stayed where it was until I leaned closer.

“Do you still think that?” he asked.

“No.” I looked at the people setting chairs around the square. “Not tonight.”

He slipped an arm around me.

The storm had left work for tomorrow. We didn't have to do all of it tonight.

For now, I listened to the people planning supper. I heard Anya laughing because the pot had survived. I heard Neri calling for clean towels. I heard Maui offer to carry a crate without pretending he had invented crates.

The vale was still there.

So was I.
